Online Casino Canada: Where It's Legal And How Each Province Works

Online casino legality in Canada is set by each province. Ontario (through AGCO and iGaming Ontario) and Alberta (through the Alberta iGaming Corporation, or AiGC) license private operators, most other provinces run a single Crown site, and offshore operators sit outside both systems. This guide maps every province and territory and explains what each model means for you.

How Online Gambling Works in Canada: Two Market Models

The Criminal Code leaves gambling to the provinces, so each one decides who can offer real-money casino games online. The result is two distinct models operating at the same time.

	Privately licensed	Crown-operated
How it works	Province licenses commercial operators to offer real-money games	A provincial Crown corporation runs the only legal site itself
Where	Ontario, Alberta	BC, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Quebec, NB, NS, PEI, NL
Who regulates	AGCO and iGaming Ontario; AGLC and AiGC (Alberta)	BCLC, Manitoba Liquor & Lotteries, SIGA/SaskGaming, Loto-Québec, Atlantic Lottery
Operator choice	Many	One
Player protections	Provincially mandated RG tools, dispute process, advertising standards	Provincially mandated RG tools, dispute process
Advertising rules	Strict; inducement restrictions apply	Crown-controlled

 

Privately licensed

Ontario and Alberta let commercial brands apply to operate under provincial rules. In Ontario, AGCO registers operators and sets the standards they must meet, while iGaming Ontario, a separate provincial agency, contracts with them and manages the market. Alberta follows a similar split between the AGLC and the AiGC, and keeps its own Crown site running alongside the private operators.

Crown-operated

In the other eight provinces, a single government-owned corporation is the only legal online option. BC, Manitoba and Saskatchewan all use the PlayNow platform built by BCLC, Quebec has Loto-Québec, and the four Atlantic provinces share Atlantic Lottery. You get one site, one game library and one set of rules.

Offshore

Sites licensed in other jurisdictions accept Canadian players in every province, including regulated ones. They answer to their overseas licence, not to a Canadian body, which matters most when something goes wrong.

Play-money social casinos sit outside all three models. They use virtual currency rather than real-money wagers and are not licensed as gambling sites.

Online Casino Canada by Province: Full Legal Breakdown

Every province and territory falls into one of three groups. Use the table to find yours, then read the short summary below it.

Province / Territory	Model	Regulator / operator	Legal online option	Min. age
Ontario	Privately licensed	AGCO / iGaming Ontario	Licensed commercial operators + OLG.ca	19
Alberta	Privately licensed (hybrid)	AGLC / Alberta iGaming Corporation (AiGC)	Licensed commercial operators + PlayAlberta	18
British Columbia	Crown-operated	BCLC	PlayNow.com	19
Manitoba	Crown-operated	Manitoba Liquor & Lotteries	PlayNow.com	18
Saskatchewan	Crown-operated	SIGA / SaskGaming (BCLC platform)	PlayNow.com	19
Quebec	Crown-operated	Loto-Québec	lotoquebec.com	18
New Brunswick	Crown-operated	Atlantic Lottery Corporation	ALC.ca	19
Nova Scotia	Crown-operated	Atlantic Lottery Corporation	ALC.ca	19
Prince Edward Island	Crown-operated	Atlantic Lottery Corporation	ALC.ca	18
Newfoundland & Labrador	Crown-operated	Atlantic Lottery Corporation	ALC.ca	19
Yukon	No provincial iGaming	Western Canada Lottery Corporation	Lottery products only	19
Northwest Territories	No provincial iGaming	Western Canada Lottery Corporation	Lottery products only	19
Nunavut	No provincial iGaming	Western Canada Lottery Corporation	Lottery products only	19
Privately Licensed Markets: Ontario and Alberta
Ontario

Ontario opened Canada’s first open, multi-operator market. The work is split between two bodies: the AGCO registers operators and enforces its standards, and iGaming Ontario contracts with them and publishes the list of authorized sites. That split is the reason every online casino Ontario players can legally use must appear on iGO’s list. OLG.ca, the province’s own Crown site, competes alongside them. Players must be 19 or older.

Alberta

Alberta launched its regulated market more recently and uses a hybrid model. The AGLC regulates gaming and registers operators, while the Alberta iGaming Corporation conducts and manages the private market. PlayAlberta, the province’s own site, stays open alongside licensed brands. The approved-operator list changes often, so check the AiGC’s current list rather than relying on a fixed number. Our Alberta online casino hub covers the market in full, and our guide to Alberta gambling laws explains the legal framework. Players must be 18 or older.

Crown-Operated Markets: BC, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Quebec and Atlantic Canada
British Columbia

British Columbia offers online casino games through PlayNow.com, run by BCLC. It is the only legal online casino in the province. Minimum age is 19.

Manitoba

Manitoba uses the same PlayNow.com platform under Manitoba Liquor & Lotteries. Players must be 18 or older.

Saskatchewan

Saskatchewan also runs on PlayNow.com. SIGA holds the exclusive right to offer online gaming, with SaskGaming operating the site on BCLC’s platform. Minimum age is 19.

Quebec

Quebec has one legal online casino, lotoquebec.com, run by Loto-Québec. Whether the province should open its market to private operators is an active political debate, but for now the Crown site is the only regulated choice. Players must be 18 or older.

Atlantic Canada

New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland & Labrador share Atlantic Lottery, which offers casino games, lottery and sports betting at ALC.ca. The minimum age is 19 in most of the region.

Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut have no territorial online casino. Residents can buy lottery products through the Western Canada Lottery Corporation, but there is no regulated real-money casino site. Any real-money casino site reachable there is offshore, with the trade-offs covered in the next section.

Provincial rules change regularly. Follow our Canadian gambling news for updates as markets open, expand or shift policy.

Regulated vs. Offshore Sites: What the Difference Actually Means

The practical difference is recourse. A provincially regulated site answers to a Canadian body that can step in if a payout is withheld or a complaint goes unresolved. An offshore site answers only to the jurisdiction that licensed it, if any.
